readings.c3s1:
¶
'''welt<sup>4</sup>†.''' Preterit of ''walt''.

'''welt-cutter''' (welt′kut″ėr), ''n.'' In ''shoe-manuf.'', a machine to cut notches in the edges of a welt, in order to admit of laying it in smoothly at the toe. The cutting-blade is triangular, and is depressed by a treadle and raised by a spring. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''welte†.''' Preterit of ''weld''<sup>3</sup>, ''welde'', older forms of ''wield''.

'''welter''' (wel′tėr), ''v.'' [< ME. ''welteren'', a var. of ''walteren'', ''waltren'', roll over: see ''walter''.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To roll or toss; tumble about; flow or act waveringly, confusedly, or tumultuously: used chiefly of waves, or of things comparable to them.
{{smaller block|<poem>Again the reckless and the brave
Ride lords of ''weltering'' seas.</poem>
{{right|''Motherwell'', Battle-Flag of Sigurd.}}
<poem>Incapable of change,
Nor touched by ''welterings'' of passion.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Prel., vi.}}
<poem>The waves
Whelmed the degraded race, and ''weltered'' o’er their graves.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', The Ages, st. 18.}}}}
'''2.''' To roll about, as in some fluid or unstable medium; be tossed or tumbled; hence, to wallow or grovel (in something).
{{smaller block|<poem>He must not float upon his watery bier
Unwept, and ''welter'' to the parching wind
Without the meed of some melodious tear.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Lycidas, l. 13.}}
<poem>Happier are they that ''welter'' in their sin,
Swine in the mud, that cannot see for slime.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Holy Grail.}}}}

¶
'''welter-weight''' (wel′tėr-wāt), ''n.'' [Appar. < ''welter'', ''v.'', + ''weight''; in allusion to the heavier motion. But in early racing-lists the first element is said to be ''swelter'', for which then ''welter'' would be a substitute. ''Swelter'' would allude to the overheating of the heavily weighted horses.] In ''horse-racing'', an unusually heavy weight, especially as carried by horses in many steeplechases and hurdle-races. These weights sometimes amount to as much as 40 pounds over weight for age.

'''welt-guide''' (welt′gīd), ''n.'' An attachment to a shoe-sewing machine for presenting the welt in the machine in position for sewing in.

'''welting''' (wel′ting), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''welt''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' A sewed border or edging; a thickened edging.—'''2.''' A severe beating with a whip, stick, strap, or the like. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|He bewhimpered his ''welting'', and I scarce thought it enough for him.
{{right|''G. Meredith.''}}}}

'''welt-leather''' (welt′leᴛ̵ʜ″ėr), ''n.'' Leather from the shoulders of tanned hides, used for making the welts of boots and shoes.
{{smaller block|The demand for ''welt leather'' is greater than the supply.
{{right|''U. S. Cons. Rep.'', No. lix. (1885), p. 442.}}}}

'''welt-machine''' (welt′ma-shēn″), ''n.'' In ''shoe-manuf.'', a machine for cutting leather into strips suitable for welts. {{smaller|The welts are afterward passed through the welt-cutter. Welts may also be cut and trimmed with hand-tools called ''welt-trimmers''.}}

'''welt-shoulders''' (welt′shōl″dėrz), ''n. pl.'' Same as ''welt-leather''.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|well-wisher|6878|welt-shoulders}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|It heartens the Young Libertine, and confirms the ''well-wishers'' to Atheism.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 190.}}}}

'''well-won''' (wel′wun), ''a.'' Honestly gained; hardly earned.
{{smaller block|My bargains and my ''well-won'' thrift.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 3. 51.}}}}

'''well-worn''' (wel′wōrn), ''a.'' '''1.''' Much affected by wear or use; hence, familiar from frequent repetition; worn threadbare.
{{smaller block|The ''well-worn'' plea that unequal acquaintanceships never prosper. {{right|''Mrs. Gore'', Two Aristocracies, xv.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Down which a ''well-worn'' pathway courted us.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Gardener’s Daughter.}}}}
'''2.''' Properly or becomingly worn; suitably borne or maintained. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>That ''well-worn'' reserve which proved he knew
No sympathy with that familiar crew.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Lara, i. 27.}}}}

'''welly''' (wel′i), ''adv.''   [An extension of ''well''<sup>2</sup>.]   Well-nigh; very nearly; almost. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Our Joseph ’s ''welly'' blind, poor lad.</poem>
{{right|''Waugh’s Lancashire Songs.''}}}}

'''welm†''', ''v. i.''   [ME. ''welmen'', < ''welm'', ''walm'', a bubbling up, a spring: see ''walm''.]   To well; spring.
{{smaller block|<poem>The watere is evere fresh and newe
That ''welmeth'' up with wawis brighte.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 1561.}}}}

'''wels''' (welz), ''n.'' The sheatfish, ''Silurus glanis.''

'''Welsh'''<sup>1</sup> (welsh), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [Formerly also ''Welch'', early mod. E. also ''Walsh''; < ME. ''Welsce'', ''Walshe'', ''Wælsce'', ''Walsche'', ''Walse'', ''Walisc'', ''Welisc'', < AS. ''welisc'', ''wælisc'', foreign, esp. Celtic, in later use applied also to the French (= OHG. ''walhisc'', foreign, esp. pertaining to Rome, Roman, MHG. ''welsch'', ''wellisch'', ''walhisc'', pertaining to Rome, French, Italian, G. ''wälsch'', foreign (cf. G. ''Wälschland'', Italy), = Icel. ''valskr'', foreign), < ''wealh'' (pl. ''wealas''), foreigner, esp. the Celts or Welshmen, = OHG. ''walh'', MHG. ''walch'', a foreigner, esp. a Roman (cf. ''Wallach''); cf. LL. ''Volcæ'', a reflex of a Celtic name. The AS. noun, in the pl. ''Wealas'', lit. ‘foreigners,’ exists in the patrial names ''Wales'', ''Cornwall'', and in comp. in ''walnut;'' and the adj. appears as a surname in the forms ''Welsh'', ''Welch'', ''Walsh''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1†.''' Foreign. See ''welshnut''.—'''2.''' Relating or pertaining to Wales (a titular principality and a part of the island of Great Britain, opposite the southern part of Ireland), or to its people or its indigenous Cymric language.{{smaller|—'''Welsh clearwing''', ''Trochilium scoliæforme'', a British hawk-moth whose larva feeds on the birch.—'''Welsh drake†''', the gadwall or gray duck, ''Chaulelasmus streperus''.   ''J. P. Giraud'', 1844. Also called ''German duck''. See cut under ''Chaulelasmus''. [New Jersey.]—'''Welsh glave'''. See ''glave'', 3.—'''Welsh groin''', in ''arch.'', a groin formed by the intersection of two cylindrical vaults, of which one is of less height than the other. See ''underpitch groining'', under ''groining''.—'''Welsh harp'''. See ''harp''.—'''Welsh hook''', an old military weapon of the bill kind, but having, in addition to a cutting-blade, a hook at the back.}}
{{smaller block|Swore the devil his true liegeman upon the cross of a ''Welsh hook''.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4. 372.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Welsh lay'''. See ''lay''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Welsh main''', a match at cock-fighting where all must fight to death.   ''Scott''.—'''Welsh medlar'''. Same as ''azarole''.—'''Welsh mortgage'''. See ''mortgage''.—'''Welsh mutton''', a choice and delicate quality of mutton obtained from a small breed of sheep in Wales.   ''Simmonds.''—'''Welsh onion''', the cibol, ''Allium fistulosum'': so called from the German ''Wälsch'', which merely indicates a foreign origin. See ''cibol'', 2, and ''leek''.—'''Welsh parsley†''', a burlesque name for hemp or a hangman’s halter made of it.}}
{{smaller block|This is a rascal deserves . . . to dance in hemp Derrick’s coranto: let’s choke him with ''Welsh parsley''.
{{right|''Randolph'', Hey for Honesty, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Welsh poppy.''' See ''Meconopsis'' and ''poppy''.—'''Welsh rabbit, ware, wig,''' etc. See the nouns.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' Collectively, as a plural word with the definite article, the people of Wales, or the members of the Cymric race indigenous to Wales. They were ruled by petty princes, and maintained their independence of the English till 1282–3.—'''2.''' The language of Wales or of the Welsh. {{smaller|The Welsh is a member of the Celtic family of languages, forming, with the Breton language and the now extinct Cornish branch, the Cymric group.}}

'''welsh<sup>2</sup>''' (welsh), ''v. t.'' and ''i.''   [Also ''welch''; < ''Welsh''<sup>1</sup>, either from the surname, or in allusion to the alleged bad faith of Welshmen.]   To cheat or practise cheating by betting or taking money as a stake on a horse-race, and running off without settling.
{{smaller block|A late decision of the Courts has rather taken the lower class of bookmaker by surprise—''welshing'' was decided to be an indictable offence. ''Nineteenth Century'', XXVI. 859.

He stakes his money with one of the book-makers whom he has seen at his stand for many years, with the certainty that he will receive his winnings, and run no risk of being ''welshed''.
{{right|''Daily Telegraph'', March 12, 1887. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''welsher''' (wel′shėr), ''n.''   [< ''welsh''<sup>2</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   A swindling better or book-maker on a race-track; one who absconds without paying his losses, or what is due to others on account of money deposited with him for betting. Also written ''welcher.''
{{smaller block|The ''welcher'' properly so called takes the money offered him to back a horse, but, when he has taken money enough from his dupes, departs from the scene of his labours, and trusts to his luck, a dyed wig, or a pair of false whiskers not to be recognised. {{right|''All the Year Round.''}}}}

'''Welshman''' (welsh′man), ''n.''; pl. ''Welshmen'' (-men).   [Formerly also ''Welchman''; < ''Welsh'' + ''man.'']   '''1.''' A native of the principality of Wales, or a member of the Welsh race.—'''2.''' A local name of the black-bass and of the squirrel-fish.

'''welshnut†''' (welsh′nut), ''n.''   [Also ''walshnut''; < ME. ''welshnote, walshnote,'' lit. ‘foreign nut’: see ''Welsh''<sup>1</sup> and ''nut,'' and cf. ''walnut.'']   The nut of ''Juglans regia,'' the European walnut; also, the tree.
{{smaller block|<poem>I saugh him carien a wind-melle
Under a ''walsh-note'' [var. ''welsh-note''] shale.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 1281.}}}}
{{smaller block|[Early printed editions have ''walnote.'']}}

'''welsome†''' (wel′sum), ''a.''   [< ME. ''welsum''; < ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''-some.'']   Well off; in good condition; prosperous.   ''Wyclif'', Gen. xxiv. 21.

'''welsomely†''' (wel′sum-li), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''welsumli''; < ''welsome'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   Prosperously; with favor or well-being.
{{smaller block|I . . . shall be turned agen ''welsumly'' to the hows of my fader. {{right|''Wyclif'', Gen. xxviii. 21.}}}}

'''welt<sup>1</sup>†''' (welt), ''v. i.''   [< ME. ''welten'', roll, upset, overturn, < AS. ''wyltan'', roll, etc., = OHG. ''walzan'', MHG. ''welzen'', G. ''walzen'', ''wälzen'' = Icel. ''velta'', roll: see ''walt''.]   To roll; revolve.

{{smaller block|Hit walz a wenyng vnwar [foolish] that ''welt'' in his mynde.
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), iii. 115.}}}}

'''welt<sup>2</sup>''' (welt), ''n.''   [< ME. ''welte'', a narrow strip of leather round a shoe, a hem, a fringe; perhaps < W. ''gwald'', a hem, welt, ''gwaltes'', the welt of a shoe (cf. ''gwaldu'', welt, hem, ''gwalteisio'', form a welt).]   '''1.''' An applied hem, selvage, bordering, or fringe; especially, a strengthening or ornamenting strip of material fastened along an edge, or over or between two joined edges, often forming a rounded ridge by the insertion of a cord or the doubling outward of the material. [Now rare, except in specific or technical uses.]

{{smaller block|Little low hedges, round like ''welts'', with some pretty pyramids, I like well. {{right|''Bacon'', Gardens (ed. 1887).}}}}
{{smaller block|Clap but a civil gown with a ''welt'' [a civilian’s gown with a furred border] on the one, and a canonical cloke with sleeves on the other. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Epicœne, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|A committee-man’s clerk, or some such excellent rascal, clothing himself from top to toe in knavery, without a ''welt'' or gard of goodness about him.
{{right|''Randolph'', Hey for Honesty, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>His coat was greene,
With ''welts'' of white seamde betweene.</poem>
{{right|''Greene'', Mourning Garment.}}}}

{{smaller block|Specifically—(''a'') In a heraldic achievement, a narrow border to an ordinary or charge. (''b'') A strip of material sewed round or along an open edge, as of a glove.}}

{{smaller block|He [a glove-maker] cuts pieces for the thumbs . . . and for the binding round the top and the opening just above the palm of the hand, which are called ''welts''. {{right|''Chambers’s Journal'', 5th ser., III. 226.}}}}
{{smaller block|(''c'') A strip of leather in a boot or shoe sewed round the edge of the conjoined upper leather and inner sole, preparatory to the attachment of the bottom or outer sole. See cut under ''boot''. (''d'') In ''carp.'', a strip forming an additional thickness laid over a flush seam or joint, or placed in an angle, to strengthen it, as in a carvel-built vessel. (''e'') In ''sheet-iron work'', a strip riveted to two contiguous plates forming a butt-joint. (''f'') In ''knitting'': (1) One of the ribs at an end of the work, intended to prevent it from rolling up, as around the opening or top of a sock. (2) A separate flap, as a heel-piece, on any piece of work made in a knitting-machine. It is made independently of the work, and afterward knitted on.}}
Hence—'''2.''' A low superficial ridge or linear swelling, as on the skin; a weal or wale: as, to raise ''welts'' on a person or an animal by blows with a whip. See ''welt''<sup>2</sup>, ''v. t.'', 2. [Colloq.]

'''welt'''<sup>2</sup> (welt), ''v. t.''   [< ''welt''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'']   '''1.''' To fix a welt or welts to or in; furnish or ornament with anything called a welt: as, to ''welt'' shoes.
{{smaller block|If any be sicke, a speare is set vp in his Tent with blacke Felt ''welted'' about it, and from thenceforth no stranger entereth therein. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 412.}}}}
{{smaller block|Wit’s as suitable to guarded coats as wisdom is to ''welted'' gowns. {{right|''Chapman'', Monsieur D’Olive, iv. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' To beat severely with a whip or stick, whereby welts may be raised. See ''welt''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'', 2. [Colloq.]—'''Welted thistle.''' {{smaller|See ''thistle''.}}

'''welt'''<sup>3</sup> (welt), ''v. i.''   [A dial. var. of ''wilt''.]   To wilt; wither; become soft or flabby, as from decay; become ropy or stringy, as some liquors. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|Her coodn’t lave ’ouze by raison of the Christmas bakkon comin’ on, and zome o’ the cider ''welted''. {{right|''R. D. Blackmore'', Lorna Doone, ii.}}}}

'''welt<sup>4</sup>†.''' Preterit of ''walt''.

'''welt-cutter''' (welt′kut″ėr), ''n.'' In ''shoe-manuf.'', a machine to cut notches in the edges of a welt, in order to admit of laying it in smoothly at the toe. The cutting-blade is triangular, and is depressed by a treadle and raised by a spring.   ''E. H. Knight.''

'''welte†.''' Preterit of ''weld''<sup>3</sup>, ''welde'', older forms of ''wield''.

'''welter''' (wel′tėr), ''v.''   [< ME. ''welteren'', a var. of ''walteren'', ''waltren'', roll over: see ''walter''.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To roll or toss; tumble about; flow or act waveringly, confusedly, or tumultuously: used chiefly of waves, or of things comparable to them.
{{smaller block|<poem>Again the reckless and the brave
Ride lords of ''weltering'' seas.</poem>
{{right|''Motherwell'', Battle-Flag of Sigurd.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Incapable of change,
Nor touched by ''welterings'' of passion.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Prel., vi.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The waves
Whelmed the degraded race, and ''weltered'' o’er their graves.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', The Ages, st. 18.}}}}
'''2.''' To roll about, as in some fluid or unstable medium; be tossed or tumbled; hence, to wallow or grovel (in something).
{{smaller block|<poem>He must not float upon his watery bier
Unwept, and ''welter'' to the parching wind
Without the meed of some melodious tear.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Lycidas, l. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Happier are they that ''welter'' in their sin,
Swine in the mud, that cannot see for slime.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Holy Grail.}}}}

'''3.''' To be exposed to or affected by some weltering or floating substance or medium: said of objects at rest.

<poem>When all is past, it is humbling to tread
O’er the ''weltering'' field of the tombless dead.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Byron'', Siege of Corinth, xvii.}}}}

{{smaller block|We climbed over the crest of high sand, where the rushes lay ''weltering'' after the wind.
{{right|''R. D. Blackmore'', Maid of Sker, xi.}}}}

{{smaller block|She fell from her horse, slain, and ''weltering'' in her blood.
{{right|''E. W. Lane'', Modern Egyptians, II. 153.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To roll; cause to turn or revolve.

{{smaller block|He that ''weltereth'' a stone. ''Bible of'' 1549 (Prov. xxvi. 27).}}

'''2.''' To subject to or affect by weltering; accomplish by or as if by wallowing. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|''Weltering'' your way through chaos and the murk of Hell.
{{right|''Carlyle.''}}}}

'''welter''' (wel′tėr), ''n.''   [< ''welter'', ''v.'']   Rolling or wallowing motion; a tossing or tumbling about; hence, turmoil; ferment; hurly-burly.

{{smaller block|The foul ''welter'' of our so-called religious or other controversies.
{{right|''Carlyle.''}}}}

{{smaller block|Nothing but a confused ''welter'' and quiver of mingled air, and rain, and spray, as if the very atmosphere is writhing in the clutches of the gale.
{{right|''Kingsley'', Two Years Ago, iii.}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''welter'' of the waters rose up to his chin.
{{right|''William Morris'', Sigurd, i.}}}}

'''welter-race''' (wel′tėr-rās), ''n.'' A race in which the horses carry welter-weight. See ''welter-weight.''

'''welter-stakes''' (wel′tėr-stāks), ''n. pl.'' The stakes in a welter-race.

'''welter-weight''' (wel′tėr-wāt), ''n.''   [Appar. < ''welter'', ''v.'', + ''weight''; in allusion to the heavier motion. But in early racing-lists the first element is said to be ''swelter'', for which then ''welter'' would be a substitute. ''Swelter'' would allude to the overheating of the heavily weighted horses.]   In ''horse-racing'', an unusually heavy weight, especially as carried by horses in many steeplechases and hurdle-races. These weights sometimes amount to as much as 40 pounds over weight for age.

'''welt-guide''' (welt′gīd), ''n.'' An attachment to a shoe-sewing machine for presenting the welt in the machine in position for sewing in.

'''welting''' (wel′ting), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''welt''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' A sewed border or edging; a thickened edging.—'''2.''' A severe beating with a whip, stick, strap, or the like. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|He bewhimpered his ''welting'', and I scarce thought it enough for him.
{{right|''G. Meredith.''}}}}

'''welt-leather''' (welt′leᴛ̵ʜ″ėr), ''n.'' Leather from the shoulders of tanned hides, used for making the welts of boots and shoes.
{{smaller block|The demand for ''welt leather'' is greater than the supply.
{{right|''U. S. Cons. Rep.'', No. lix. (1885), p. 442.}}}}

'''welt-machine''' (welt′ma-shēn″), ''n.'' In ''shoe-manuf.'', a machine for cutting leather into strips suitable for welts. {{smaller|The welts are afterward passed through the welt-cutter. Welts may also be cut and trimmed with hand-tools called ''welt-trimmers''.}}

'''welt-shoulders''' (welt′shōl″dėrz), ''n. pl.'' Same as ''welt-leather''.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
